testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Results of fee patents at Shoshone Indian Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 303 fee patents issued 1907-1930 at Shoshone Reservation averaging 80 acres of good irrigable agricultural land. Approximately 90% of recipients either sold or mortgaged their lands. Some few made beneficial use of proceeds through purchase of livestock and agricultural equipment. Recommends against issuing patents without individual examination and recommends holding back not less than 160 acres as the reservation is not adapted for farming. Cautions against granting patents to females as their property is soon squandered by husbands, desertions are frequent, and women are left with small children without means of support.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Effects of releasing Indians from Government control at Cheyenne & Arapaho Agency
testimony.key_claims: In practically every case lands have been sold. A great many used proceeds unwisely; possibly a majority used proceeds for improvement of other family lands or investment in other business. Believes beneficial to give able-bodied competent Indians their patents. Recommends examining each individual case as to age, opportunity and physical capacity. After Indian receives patent, agency officials do not follow up their activities and Indians resent any effort to find out what they are doing with lands or proceeds. Agency officials often have only general knowledge of consequences of patents. Notes Indians frequently say the Government turned them loose and see no reason for further oversight.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Results of 613 fee patents at Yankton Sioux Reservation
testimony.key_claims: 599 full allotment patents and 13 partial issued. Originally 3113 allotments comprising 368,400 acres on reservation. Approximately half of patents issued prior to 1916, some by special Act of Congress. Secretary of Interior visited in May 1916 and delivered 186 patents based on Competency Commission report. About 100 more issued under Declaration of Policy. Not to exceed 10 of 613 recipients own entire original allotment; perhaps not to exceed 50 own any portion. Approximately 550 have disposed of all land; approximately 400 have absolutely nothing to show. Only 59,000 acres remain in trust. Allotments ranged 80-320 acres; heads of families received 160 acres agricultural or 320 acres grazing; minors received 80 acres agricultural or 160 acres grazing; full-bloods received 60 acres. Mixed-bloods used sharp practice to have allotments classified as grazing land to obtain twice the acreage. About 80% of reservation land is excellent agricultural land. Indians typically dispose of land almost immediately after receiving patents, usually within 12 months. Primary means of squandering: purchase of automobiles, beset by white men at below-adequate prices. Approximately 60% of able-bodied members farm to some extent. Recommends either refuse to issue patents to any part of allotments or issue to all; no partial releases.

testimony.witness_title: United States Indian Farmer, Yankton Indian Reservation
testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Views on releasing Santee and Yankton Sioux from Government supervision based on field experience
testimony.key_claims: Does not advocate turning Indians loose irrespective of qualifications but believes each case should receive careful consideration. Every young able-bodied Indian whose mind is functioning properly should have everything turned over unrestricted. Does not believe in reserving part of allotment as safety net. Indian should either be full citizen or ward with no compromise. Young Indians who are not able-bodied or weak-minded, and all old and indigent ones, should remain under supervision. Many will squander everything in a year or two but if still able to work they will make better citizens. Cites Joseph Ellis and Thomas Hunter of Lake Andes, and Robert Medicinehorn and Mark Patterson of Watertown area as examples of successful fee patent holders among Yankton Sioux. Cites Simon Vasser and Gilbert St. Pierre of Wagner as other examples.

testimony.hearing: Board of Indian Commissioners Survey - Bulletin No. 138
testimony.subject: Policy on patents-in-fee and competency at Rosebud Agency
testimony.key_claims: Approximately 600 fee patents issued under this agency, records not kept up to date. About 90% of patent recipients immediately sold allotments or mortgaged and sold when mortgage came due. 85% of allotments were 160 acres, ranging in value from $1000 to $16,000 with average of about $4000 per quarter section. Opposes granting patents in bulk; every case should be decided on its merits irrespective of blood status or educational qualifications. An Indian can be competent to earn a living but not competent to manage $10,000-$15,000 property. Not to exceed one Indian in ten who receives patent uses proceeds for productive purposes such as teams, farm implements, or home improvements. Recommends Office outline a standard for Competency Commissioner and Superintendents to follow. Indian should be given full control of property without governmental supervision when competent but not before.
